package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed via installers and phishing sites, not a software package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: CopperStealth / CopperPhish is a sophisticated malware campaign that leverages deceptive installers and phishing websites to infect victims. The malware injects payloads into system processes, deploys rootkits for persistence and evasion, blocks security software, exfiltrates personal and financial data, and orchestrates large-scale credential and credit card phishing attacks. It employs multiple evasion and anti-forensics techniques, including rootkit drivers, process injection, registry manipulation, and custom phishing browsers, making it highly dangerous and difficult to detect.

execution_context.file_location: malicious installer (downloaded from software sharing website)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Encoded URLs in installer → decode → download CopperStealth dropper → execute dropper
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At installation time, the installer decodes embedded URLs, downloads the CopperStealth dropper from remote servers, and executes the dropper, resulting in the initial infection and enabling further malicious payload deployment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The installer performs hidden network operations to download and execute additional payloads from obfuscated URLs, which is a common malware delivery tactic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers only install the advertised software and do not silently fetch or execute hidden binaries from encoded or obfuscated sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Auto-updaters may fetch updates, but only with user consent, visible progress, and cryptographic integrity checks.
key_indicators: Encoded or obfuscated URLs embedded in installer
Silent download and execution of additional binaries without user notification
Network activity to untrusted or suspicious domains during installation

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Rootkit driver with IRP_MJ_CREATE, IRP_MJ_READ, IRP_MJ_SHUTDOWN handlers; injects payloads into explorer.exe and other processes.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After installation, at system startup or post-install, the rootkit driver registers as a file system filter, handles IRP_MJ_CREATE/READ/SHUTDOWN requests, injects code into explorer.exe and other system processes, and blocks execution of certain drivers and access to registry keys, resulting in persistent system compromise and evasion of security tools.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The driver exhibits classic rootkit behavior, including process injection and interference with system and security operations, which are hallmarks of advanced malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate drivers do not inject code into unrelated processes or block the operation of security software and system components.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some security products use filter drivers, but these operate transparently, with user consent and without interfering with unrelated processes.
key_indicators: Process injection into explorer.exe and other system processes
Registration as a file system filter driver with IRP_MJ_CREATE/READ/SHUTDOWN handlers
Blocking of security vendor drivers and registry key access

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: DriverEntry: if blacklisted byte sequence found in driver, modify entry point to return STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At driver load time, the rootkit scans loaded drivers for blacklisted byte sequences associated with security vendors, and if detected, modifies the driver's entry point to immediately return STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED, thereby sabotaging the loading of security software.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code actively sabotages security software by preventing their drivers from loading, which is a direct anti-AV and anti-forensics technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal drivers do not interfere with the loading or operation of other drivers, especially those belonging to security vendors.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for sabotaging other drivers in this manner; this is exclusively malicious behavior.
key_indicators: Scanning for blacklisted byte sequences in loaded drivers
Modification of driver entry points to force STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED
Targeted blocking of security vendor drivers

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Increase HKCU\Software\Microsoft\count_a0b1c2d3; check internet via hxxp://www.msftconnecttest.com/connecttest.txt; report to hxxp://cnzz_url&m=<machine ID>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the statistics module increments a registry counter at HKCU\Software\Microsoft\count_a0b1c2d3, checks for internet connectivity by accessing hxxp://www.msftconnecttest.com/connecttest.txt, collects a unique machine ID, and exfiltrates this data to a remote telemetry server, enabling victim tracking and campaign monitoring.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The module silently modifies the registry and exfiltrates unique machine identifiers to a third-party server without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not silently report unique machine IDs or modify registry keys for tracking without explicit user consent and a clear privacy policy.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software collects telemetry, but always with user consent, transparency, and opt-out options.
key_indicators: Silent modification of HKCU\Software\Microsoft\count_a0b1c2d3 registry key
Outbound connection to suspicious telemetry server (cnzz)
Collection and exfiltration of unique machine identifiers

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Web browser program uses Internet Explorer object and SHDocVwCtl class to extract 'checkcode' input and send exit message via pipes if correct.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the phishing browser launches a custom window using the Internet Explorer object and SHDocVwCtl class, collects user input for a 'checkcode' field, and communicates with the main malware payload via inter-process pipes to control process flow based on victim interaction, facilitating the phishing attack.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of a custom browser window to collect sensitive input and control malware persistence is a strong indicator of phishing and malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate browsers do not control malware payloads or require users to enter confirmation codes for network restoration, nor do they prevent window closure or minimize options.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate software uses custom browser windows in this manner for credential collection and process control.
key_indicators: Custom browser window with no close or minimize controls
Collection of sensitive user input (confirmation code)
Inter-process communication to control malware persistence

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: HTML form requesting cardholder name, credit card number, expiration date, CVV, address, phone, etc.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon user interaction, the phishing webpage presents an HTML form that mimics a Microsoft page, requests sensitive credit card and personal information, and submits the collected data to the attacker's server, resulting in credential and financial data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The webpage impersonates Microsoft and requests full credit card and personal details, which is a classic phishing tactic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Microsoft or network restoration pages never request full credit card details or sensitive personal information for service restoration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use case exists for requesting such sensitive information in this context; this is purely fraudulent.
key_indicators: Collection of full credit card and personal details
Use of suspicious or non-Microsoft domains

attack_chain.action: Victim downloads malicious installer from a software sharing website.
Installer decodes embedded URLs, downloads the CopperStealth dropper, and executes it.
CopperStealth rootkit installs as a file system filter driver, injects payloads into system processes, and blocks security software.
Statistics module collects machine ID, checks internet connectivity, and exfiltrates data to remote server.
CopperPhish phishing browser is launched, presenting fake Microsoft pages to the victim.
Victim is tricked into entering sensitive credit card and personal information on the phishing page.

behavioral_signatures: Installer decoding and downloading additional payloads from encoded or obfuscated URLs during installation
Rootkit driver registering as a file system filter and injecting code into explorer.exe and other system processes
Blocking of security vendor drivers via blacklisted byte sequence scanning and entry point modification
Silent registry modification at HKCU\Software\Microsoft\count_a0b1c2d3 and outbound telemetry to suspicious domains
Custom browser windows with no close/minimize controls, collecting sensitive input and communicating with malware payloads
Phishing pages impersonating Microsoft and requesting full credit card and personal details on suspicious domains
file_indicators: Presence of unknown or unsigned drivers with IRP_MJ_CREATE/READ/SHUTDOWN handlers
Installer files containing encoded or obfuscated URLs
Phishing browser executables utilizing SHDocVwCtl class and Internet Explorer COM objects
network_indicators: Phishing domains such as 0zpt4.za.com, newappsofthq.site, pharmadescuento.com
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for installer processes that decode and download additional payloads from encoded or obfuscated URLs. Detect registration of unknown or unsigned file system filter drivers and process injection into explorer.exe or other system processes. Flag attempts to block or sabotage security vendor drivers via byte sequence scanning and entry point modification. Watch for silent registry modifications to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\count_a0b1c2d3 and outbound connections to known telemetry and phishing domains. Identify custom browser windows that cannot be closed or minimized and collect sensitive information, especially those impersonating Microsoft. Use file, network, and behavioral IOCs to block, quarantine, and investigate affected systems.
